topic: Soyuz 11 cosmonauts killed by pressure valve failure during re-entry
niche_fit: yes - documented 1971 Soviet space disaster caused by institutional design failure and neglected safety protocols
_transcript: On the 30th of June, 1971, the Soyuz 11  spacecraft re-entered Earth’s atmosphere   after almost a month in space. On board were  three men who had been seen on television screens   across the Soviet Union, and around the world,  almost constantly for the last few weeks. They   were already considered heroes: brave cosmonauts  who had taken on a risky and difficult mission,   and spent longer in space than any human had  before. The people of the Soviet Union were   keen to welcome them back to Earth… but when  their capsule touched down and the recovery   team knocked on the door, they received no  response. Something had gone very, very wrong. The Space Race is the name given to the fierce  competition between the United States and the   Soviet Union in the mid-twentieth  Century to see which nation would   be the first to conquer space. This  intense technological rivalry is   sometimes thought to have been a substitute  for armed combat between the two powers. From the moment the Soviet Union launched its  first satellite, Sputnik, into space in 1957,   the battle for technological superiority  between them and the USA would take place   on a new frontier, high above the  Earth. Continual one-upmanship would   drive scientific discoveries and make  heroes out of astronauts in the US,   and their counterpart cosmonauts in the Soviet  Union. But being either an astronaut or a   cosmonaut during this time of rapid, urgent  progress was, at times, immensely risky. The Soviets took an early lead in the race,  following up the successful launch of Sputnik by   being the first to send a human into space: Yuri  Gagarin on the Vostok 1 space mission in 1961. As the two sides raced to get the  upper hand in the ensuing decade,   both suffered fatal tragedies. In 1967  the three-strong crew of American Apollo   1 were killed in a fire. In the same year,  cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died when the   Soviet Soyuz 1 crashed into the ground after  re-entry due to a malfunctioning parachute. Despite these disasters, both countries  continued to develop their space programs   at a breakneck pace. The following  year, 1968, saw American Apollo 7,   carry out a flawless mission to test  out the Apollo command and service   module. This great success was followed  by an even bigger one the next year when,   with the Apollo 11 mission, the United States  became the first nation to put men on the moon. The Soviet response in 1971 was to  launch the first ever Space Station,   Salyut 1. The Salyut programme went extremely  well. Indeed, the final module launched as   part of it remains in orbit to this day, as a  crucial part of the International Space Station.   However – like all space flight programmes –  this one was not without problems and setbacks. The first of these came immediately after the  initial launch, while ground crews were still   celebrating the success of Salyut 1. The  cover on Salyut 1’s telescope, it emerged,   had not detached properly… dramatically decreasing  the range of work that could be done on board   the new space station. New, different  objectives were hastily conceived instead. A few days after this, Soyuz 10 was launched, with  the intention that the three-man crew would dock   and board Salyut 1 and stay there for a month.  However, the mission was aborted when Soyuz   10 failed to dock with the space station. The crew  returned, unsuccessful in their mission, to Earth. Plans for the launch of Soyuz 11 were already  in place. Originally, the backup crew for the   Soyuz 10 mission were scheduled to fly, but  four days before the launch one of the crew,   Valeri Kubasov, felt unwell. An x-ray revealed  some slight swelling on his right lung. Doctors feared that this was a sign of  tuberculosis, and so, according to Ministry   of Health rules, the entire crew was told to  stand down. It turned out that the swelling   was due only to an allergic reaction, rather than  tuberculosis. This unfortunate misdiagnosis would   inadvertently save the lives of three crewmen,  and consign their replacements to death. The replacement Soyuz 11 crew were to  be Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov,   and Viktor Patsayev. They were launched on  the 6th of June, 1971, from a facility in   Soviet Kazakhstan. Their spaceship was,  by necessity, very small… and as such,   the crew didn’t have the space to wear  their pressure suits whilst in the capsule. The following day, the 7th of June, they  successfully docked with Salyut 1. The crew   stayed on board the space station for the next 22  days; the longest anyone had ever spent in space. They spent their time conducting experiments  and using gamma-ray telescopes to collect   data. Patsayev became the first person  to operate such a telescope in space.   They studied the weather on Earth, maintained  plants including Chinese cabbage and onions,   experimented on tadpoles, algae and flies and  conducted cardiovascular tests on themselves.   Much of this work was ground-breaking…  and it was done in a very public fashion,   too. For the first time the general public  were kept up to date with the progress of a   space mission, with the crew even featuring in  a television broadcast while orbiting Earth. Not everything went smoothly, of course.  The gruelling, monotonous shifts (which   were designed to maximise their time on the  ship with one crew member awake at all times)   caused tension. The three men had had only  days to adjust to the fact that they would   actually be going on the mission. Only one  of them, Volkov, had experienced spaceflight   before. Now they were spending more time in  space than any person in history ever had.   Mission doctors were, understandably,  concerned about their mental health. These concerns deepened when, on the 16th  of June, the crew smelled smoke. They traced   the smell to a small electrical fire, which was  extinguished with guidance from Aleksei Yeliseyev,   a veteran cosmonaut who had flown on previous  Soyuz missions, and who was acting as a crew   communicator back on Earth. The three cosmonauts  spent the night on board Soyuz 11 while the air in   the station was cleaned. A potential crisis had  been averted, but the close call left the crew   nervous. They asked if they could return to Earth  early, but ground control insisted they were safe. Almost daily television broadcasts of  their activities continued throughout   their stay on board Salyut 1. The men  became household names. Naturally,   news of tension or any setback was never  included in any broadcast. Instead,   coverage focussed on the positive.  For example, on the 19th of June,   Patsayev celebrated his 38th birthday - the first  person ever to celebrate a birthday in space. A few days later, the crew began to  prepare for their return to Earth. By the 29th of June, the crew had  packed up their payload of film   and scientific samples, and were ready to go home. The Soyuz successfully detached from  Salyut 1 and flew in co-orbit around   the Earth three times before making a re-entry  attempt. The work compartment and the service   module were both jettisoned as planned,  leaving the crew in the descent module. At this point, all communication  with the Soyuz was lost. This was worrying, but not catastrophic. The  descent was mostly an automated process. Indeed,   as the module approached the ground,  the parachute automatically deployed,   and it came in for what appeared to be  a successful landing. The recovery team   was at the scene within ten minutes, and noted  that the capsule appeared completely undamaged. However, when they knocked on the capsule,  there was no answer. When it was opened,   they discovered the three lifeless bodies of the  crew. Attempts were made to resuscitate them,   but without success. They reported the  situation back to Mission Control using a   one to five numbering system: five would convey  that a crewmember was in excellent health,   while one would convey the opposite. On  that day, the report was, “one, one, one.” The cause of death of the cosmonauts wasn’t  officially announced for nearly two years.   The mission had captured the imagination of the  public, and the government was keen to emphasise   its many successful research outcomes,  rather than the tragic loss of the crew. Over in the US, the disaster prompted fears that   the human body simply couldn’t cope with  being in space for that length of time. Eventually, though, the cause of death  became clear. The jettisoning of the   modules during descent had caused a faulty valve  to open. Air leaked rapidly out, and the crew,   unable to wear their pressure suits due to  the limited space in the capsule, died of   asphyxiation. The body of Patsayev was found close  to the valve, leading investigators to believe   that he had survived long enough to identify  the problem, but not long enough to rectify it. Alexie Leonov, who was the original commander of  the Soyuz 11 mission before the late change in   personnel, had recommended that these valves  be manually closed, as he did not trust the   automated system. Unfortunately, it seemed the  replacement crew had neglected to follow this   advice. Leonov experimented with manually shutting  the valves, and found that it took him almost one   minute – too long for the fateful crew, who would  have had only seconds to respond to the emergency. There was an outpouring of grief over the  deaths of the three cosmonauts. They were   each posthumously awarded a Hero of the Soviet  Union medal, and their bodies lay in state in   Moscow before they were given full state  funerals. Leonid Brezhnev was seen wiping   away tears as he passed their coffins in a  display considered unusual for Soviet leaders. A month after the disaster, Apollo 15  astronauts placed a memorial plaque   near their landing site on the moon. A  Soviet monument was erected in 1973 at   the place where the capsule had landed.  This was replaced by a new memorial in   2016. Craters on the moon have been  named after each of the three men. In addition to this, many lessons were learned  from the disaster. All future Soyuz were built   with sturdier valves that had quick-action  chokes for use in the event of an air leak. Now,   crews routinely wear pressure suits during  launches and landings. Every space launch   since Soyuz 11 has been made safer thanks to  the knowledge gained in the aftermath of this   tragedy. In part thanks to these advances,  the three cosmonauts lost during the return   of Soyuz 11 remain the only three people to have  ever died outside of the Earth’s atmosphere.
